newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Popular ANC rebel to form S.Africa opposition party.
newsitem.headline: Popular ANC rebel to form S.Africa opposition party.

text.p: Bantu Holomisa, a hugely popular protege of South African President Nelson Mandela who fell from favour last year, said on Monday he was confident of founding a new opposition party by June.
The party, widely seen as a possible haven for defectors from Mandela's all-powerful African National Congress, should be up and running to fight the 1999 election campaign, he said.
"We need an alternative," Holomisa told Reuters. "The ANC is not the only bull in the kraal (camp)."

The former military leader of the impoverished Transkei homeland was pushed out of the ANC last year after making public bribery allegations against a colleague and then, in what ANC leaders saw as unacceptable impudence, refusing to apologise.

The ANC rejected his request to be let back in and his alienation culminated at the weekend when he was elected head of a new consultative forum that will oversee the birth of a party whose policies are still to be hammered out.
Holomisa, 41, said the forum's members would meet again in June for a conference to found and name the party.
"We are opening the net," the former general said. "It will be an opposition party, there is no doubt about that."
In a shifting political landscape, Mandela is offering a role in government to the mostly white Democratic Party and black-led Pan Africanist Congress, two small opposition parties.
But no olive branch is likely for Holomisa from a party for which few sins are greater than internal dissent, analysts said.
South Africa's parties have been wooing one another as the new parliamentary year begins and 1999 elections loom closer.
The National Party of former president F.W. de Klerk wants to widen its narrow support base of white and coloured, or mixed-race, voters.

The "Nats" walked out of Mandela's national unity government last year saying they were being ignored, and are now the biggest opposition group. But they have had little success in luring blacks, who make up three-quarters of the electorate.
Holomisa said the NP, with its history as the party that oppressed non-whites through four decades of apartheid, was no place for blacks disillusioned with the ANC.
The ANC, in power and making difficult choices, is having problems trying to be all things to all its supporters, as it was when it was a mass movement opposed to the apartheid regime.
Its communist and trade union allies, fondly recalling the ANC's recent socialist past, are not amused by the government's market-friendly economic policies.
Personality clashes between the party establishment and more populist leaders such as Holomisa and Mandela's ex-wife Winnie, and power struggles in the regions have also caused party rifts.
But Mandela's party, which won almost two-thirds of the vote in 1994 all-race elections, is virtually ensured victory in 1999 under his heir apparent Thabo Mbeki, and probably in 2004 too.
Until now its only sizeable black-led rival has been the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party of chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, but he, like de Klerk, has failed to widen his party's appeal.
Holomisa's popularity makes him a potentially troublesome opponent to the ANC, whose grassroots members have in some places rallied in his support.
He came to power in a 1987 coup in Transkei, a rural backwater South Africa declared an independent country but the world refused to recognise, and also Mandela's home area.
Holomisa used his position not as an apartheid lackey but to further the anti-apartheid struggle of the ANC.
Mandela took him under his wing and said he was like a son, but they fell out last year, politically at least.
"I still go and see him without an appointment," Holomisa said. "At a personal level, he is still my parent."
